lab_title: Retrograde Motion: From Puzzle to Heliocentric Understanding
top_level_objectives: Understand the phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion as observed from Earth
Explain retrograde motion as a consequence of relative orbital motion rather than actual reversal of planetary motion
Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in relation to their orbital distances
Recognize how the heliocentric model elegantly accounts for retrograde motion without requiring epicycles

scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the observational puzzle by showing students how Mars appears to move across the night sky over several weeks, slowing, reversing, then resuming eastward motion.
key_visuals: Night sky dome with background constellation
Mars positioned at multiple locations along its retrograde path across constellations
Numbered timeline markers showing progression from east to west to east
Arrows or trails indicating Mars's apparent direction of motion at different points
student_actions: Observe Mars's position on successive nights spread across two months
Identify the moment when Mars slows and begins moving westward (retrograde begins)
Identify the moment when Mars stops moving backward and resumes eastward motion (retrograde ends)
Trace the overall S-shaped or looping path Mars traces against the background stars

scenes.brief_purpose: Show students how ancient astronomers explained retrograde motion using epicycles on the geocentric model, highlighting the model's complexity.
key_visuals: Geocentric diagram with stationary Earth at the center
Mars on a large circular deferent orbit around Earth
A smaller epicycle superimposed on Mars's position
Trace showing how the epicycle creates a looping path
Comparison label showing 'Complex: requires nested circular orbits'
student_actions: Observe how the epicycle motion combines with the deferent motion to produce the observed loop
Mentally compare this explanation to the retrograde pattern they observed in Scene 1
Recognize that while this model works mathematically, it feels unnecessarily complicated

scenes.scene_name: Orbital Perspective: Earth and Mars from Above
scenes.brief_purpose: Transition to a heliocentric view by showing the solar system from outside, allowing students to see Earth and Mars in their actual orbits at the same moment they observed retrograde motion on Earth.
key_visuals: Sun at the center
Earth's inner orbit (smaller) and Mars's outer orbit (larger) both drawn in 3D
Earth and Mars positioned at the moment retrograde motion begins on Earth
Orbital velocity vectors or speed indicators showing Earth moving faster than Mars
A line of sight from Earth toward Mars and the background stars beyond
student_actions: Identify which planet is closer to the Sun and moving faster
Observe Earth and Mars's relative positions at the retrograde-start moment
Mentally project a line of sight from Earth to Mars and imagine how Mars appears against the distant stars
Prepare to see how the relative motion creates the illusion of reversal

scenes.scene_name: Relative Motion Animation: The Passing Effect
scenes.brief_purpose: Animate the passage of Earth overtaking Mars and show in real time how this causes Mars to appear to reverse direction against the background star field, using a visual analogy (fast car passing a slower car).
key_visuals: Animated orbits showing Earth and Mars moving smoothly along their paths
Earth visibly gaining ground on Mars over time
A frozen perspective ray or 'line of sight' from Earth to the background stars, updating as Earth moves
Mars's projected position on a simulated star field, showing the S-shaped retrograde path emerge as Earth passes
Side-by-side car-passing analogy diagram showing the relative motion principle
student_actions: Watch the animation showing Earth overtaking Mars in the heliocentric view
Observe how Mars's position shifts on the background star field as Earth moves
Notice how the retrograde loop emerges naturally from the relative motion
Connect the car-passing analogy to the planetary motion to reinforce intuition

scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize by showing that the heliocentric relative-motion explanation produces exactly the retrograde pattern observed from Earth, validating the model.
key_visuals: Split screen: heliocentric orbits on the left, Earth-based night sky on the right
Mars's position in the heliocentric view linked to its position on the night sky view
Timeline slider or animation playback showing both views advancing together
Retrograde loop on the night sky view clearly matching the pattern from Scene 1
student_actions: Play through the animation, comparing the two perspectives
Verify that retrograde motion occurs when Earth overtakes Mars in the heliocentric view
Confirm that the loop shape and timing match what was observed in Scene 1
Articulate the insight: retrograde motion is an optical illusion of relative motion, not actual reversal

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend understanding by exploring how planets farther from the Sun exhibit less dramatic retrograde loops, reinforcing the role of orbital distance and relative velocity.
key_visuals: Heliocentric view with the Sun and orbits of Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn all displayed to scale
Animated relative-motion sequences for Jupiter and Saturn, similar to Scene 4
Retrograde loop patterns for all three planets shown side by side for visual comparison
Text labels showing orbital periods and relative velocities
student_actions: Observe how Jupiter's retrograde loop is less pronounced than Mars's
Observe how Saturn's retrograde loop is even less dramatic
Hypothesize why: farther planets orbit slower and take longer to lap in Earth's reference frame, reducing the relative-motion effect
Recognize the pattern: retrograde loop amplitude correlates with orbital distance

scenes.brief_purpose: Wrap up by having students reflect on the power of the heliocentric model to explain retrograde motion simply, and contrast it with the geocentric epicycle approach.
key_visuals: Side-by-side visual summary: geocentric epicycle diagram vs. heliocentric relative-motion diagram
Timeline or infographic showing the historical shift from geocentric to heliocentric thinking
Key insight highlighted: 'Simple motion + relative perspective = complex appearance'
student_actions: Review the two explanations (epicycles vs. relative motion) side by side
Discuss which explanation feels more intuitive and parsimonious
Reflect on how a change in reference frame (moving to the solar system view) can simplify understanding
Consider how this paradigm shift exemplifies scientific progress and the power of choosing the right frame of reference
